commit.text:
The oldest tree in the orchard had stopped casting a complete shadow. Where a branch should have darkened the dust, Sera saw sunlight lying in a pale rectangle, as if someone had already cut the wood from the world. She climbed the low wall and pressed her ear against the trunk. The old tree was still alive when Sera touched its warm bark. Its warmth was slight, and the sap moved too slowly for her to hear, but a green line appeared when she lifted the loose bark with her nail. Orin told her to leave it alone. The village had lost enough things by opening them to discover whether anything remained inside. He was carrying the new bell in both hands, taking one careful step at a time over the roots. She jumped down to move the ladder before its legs damaged the last patch of young grass.

Orin hung the bronze bell beside the oldest orchard tree. The metal had been cast from broken household vessels, and Sera could identify the lip of her mother's old cooking pot in the rough curve near the rim. Orin said he could polish it smooth. She asked him not to, at least until her mother had seen it. The old tree had survived worse summers, but the glass seeds in the library were nearly exhausted and the cistern had not held water for weeks. A bell might gather people to decide what to give. It could not itself make rain. Mael arrived wearing a ceremonial coat unsuited to the heat. The village roll identified Mael as the appointed reeve. He read the appointment line aloud from the roll he carried, as if a title might add weight to the promise he was about to make. “The rain can bring back anything,” Mael said. Sera looked towards the tree and heard Orin stop adjusting the bell rope.

Nobody argued with the reeve before the waiting villagers. Sera asked instead which memories he had arranged for the afternoon's seeds. He said the library kept enough examples for every household. Examples were written accounts, not freely offered memories, and the difference had occupied most of her apprenticeship. A seed opened only when its giver chose a true piece of remembered life and allowed the seed to take its rain from that choice. Repeating another person's words could imitate the shape of the gift without making it voluntary. Mael told her not to make a ceremony out of a simple matter. She said it was already a ceremony, and he had brought the coat. Several villagers laughed. He did not, but he walked with her towards the library rather than order her to begin beneath the tree.

Sera reached the seed library before the last bell. Fenn had set two basins on the table and covered the windows with cloth to keep the glass from heating unevenly. Fenn kept the memory book under her shawl. Its leather corner made a square beneath the wool, moving when she breathed. Sera asked whether she had brought the volume for the seed receipts or the memories. Fenn answered that everything required a receipt sooner or later. She would not open it while Mael stood beside her. A blank page remained warm inside the memory book. Sera noticed the warmth when Fenn set the closed book on the table and briefly exposed the inner edge. The other pages lay cool against one another. She asked whether something had been spilled there. Fenn said no, then moved her hand over the opening so Mael could no longer see which leaf Sera meant.

Orin carried the case to the table, but waited for Sera to unlock it. Sera entrusted the seed case to Orin. She wanted both hands free to steady the bowls, and the bellsmith had always treated fragile things with a patience that made his large fingers seem smaller. Sera knew Orin had received the seed case. Mael said he had arranged payment, a phrase Orin took to mean he had paid. Orin believed Mael had paid for the seeds, but Fenn’s receipt bore Sera’s name. The receipt named Sera's allotment and carried the mark she had made after selling her small kiln. She did not correct Orin in front of the reeve. Later she wondered whether silence had already made her a participant in a story she disliked. Sera trusted Orin with the case but not with the choice of whose memory to spend. Choosing a memory belonged to its giver. The custody of a box could not include the right to open another person's past, however usefully a bellsmith's hands could hold it.

Sera chose two small memories she could offer without giving away anybody else's confidence: the first cup she had shaped without a crack, and the sound of her mother laughing when the cup leaned to one side. She described them in her own words and touched the glass only after Fenn asked whether she wished to continue. Two seeds dissolved in the basin, leaving ten in Sera’s allotment. “Ten seeds are left,” Sera said. Rain rose from the basins and fell through a circular space in the ceiling, enough to darken the cloth over the orchard path. Mael wanted the next seed opened at once. Sera asked the waiting villagers whose memory would come next. Several looked at one another. A gift that might have been easy in private became difficult beneath an official promise. Nobody volunteered. The reeve called the silence hesitation, as if a more flattering word could turn it into consent.

One seed remained loose beside the latch. A seed rang softly without being touched. The note was too low to resemble the bell outside, yet Orin lifted his head as though someone had called his childhood name. Mael caught the seed before it rolled into the water. Mael refused to remove a silver glove. The glove covered his hand past the wrist, even while the room grew hot enough to make the ink on the receipts tacky. Sera asked him to set the seed down. He did, but not before she saw the glass brighten against the silver. Her attention slipped from the bowl she was moving. A shard of glass cut Sera’s left palm. Fenn bound the cut with a strip torn from a clean apron. The blood looked ordinary beside the strange glass, and Sera found the sight reassuring until Mael asked whether an injury could count as an offering. Fenn said pain was not permission.

They waited for the small rain to finish before discussing another seed. Sera watched a bright line move across the new bell visible through the door. Sera could not decide whether the pale mark on the bell was a letter. It could have been a letter, an uneven patch left by casting, or a reflection from Mael's coat. She wanted Orin to examine it, then saw how intently he was watching the seed that had rung. The library was becoming a room full of private recognitions. Sera remembered living in the pottery shed before she became an apprentice. She had kept clay under the bed to stop it drying too quickly and woken to her mother's feet moving around it in the dark. That room belonged to a period she could remember without dating its beginning. It was not where she lived now, and recalling it did not make her willing to spend it. Not every useful memory had to become rain simply because someone else was thirsty.

Fenn wrote the two spent seeds into the allotment book, leaving ten small circles untouched. Sera believed Fenn would keep a receipt for every seed. The old woman disliked losing money as much as she disliked losing memories, and for once those habits served the same purpose. Sera asked whether the warm blank page had a name attached to it. Fenn said the name had been scraped away before she received the book. Mael said such pages were common. Sera asked him whether he meant empty pages were common or warm ones. He answered by checking the window cloth. Orin placed the seed back in the case and fastened both catches, not only the nearer one. The sound of the second catch made Sera grateful. A person could answer a difficult room with a small, observable piece of care instead of another general promise.

She planned to spend another seed after the harvest meeting. The meeting would let each household decide privately, without the reeve standing beside an open basin. Mael objected that delay might cost the oldest tree its last living branch. Fenn answered that rain could nourish a living tree but could not revive a dead one, and a gift forced in panic would not open the seed anyway. If a borrowed memory were accepted, the orchard might owe someone rain. Sera wrote the question in the margin rather than enter a debt against any household. They needed to find out what Mael had done, not charge a neighbour for an attractive theory. Orin offered to lower the bell into the cistern, where the acoustics might explain the ringing seed. Mael said there was no need. He said it quickly enough that the proposal acquired a significance it had not possessed a moment before.

The library lamps were lit while the last villagers went home carrying empty bowls. Fenn took the memory book with her, and Orin retained the seed case as Sera had asked. Sera spread the damp window cloth on the table to dry. The small rain had helped the grass near the path, but it had not changed the orchard's need for another honest gift. She lay down on the narrow bench meant for waiting apprentices and watched the ceiling circle darken into night. She dreamed that the old tree walked into her childhood kitchen. In sleep its roots lifted the pots from the shelves without breaking them, and her mother asked whether they had invited it for supper. She woke with her bandaged hand against her cheek. Outside, the old tree stood where it had always stood. The dream had moved nothing except her fear, and the case still belonged in Orin's careful custody until morning. Sera stayed in the seed library until the lamps were lowered.

commit.text:
The cistern steps had been built for people carrying full jars, each tread wide enough for two feet and a pause. Sera went down with an empty bowl, finding the design more merciful than the village's recent conversations. Sera descended into the dry cistern. The dry floor was patterned with old water lines. A person could stand inside the outline of a summer that had once filled the chamber to the shoulders. Orin followed with the bell, lowering it a little at each step until its rim rested on a folded sack. Mael waited above, one silver glove bright against the stone. Fenn came last with the book beneath her shawl. Nobody had told her the visit was private. Nobody had found a convincing reason to ask her to leave.

Orin had carried the case through the night, refusing to let the reeve borrow a seed for a demonstration that required no witnesses. Now he needed both hands for the bell rope. Orin gave the seed case to Fenn beside the cistern steps. Fenn checked the catches without opening them. She had kept a separate seed borrowed from Sera during the spring, outside the twelve allotted for yesterday's meeting. It was still intact in its folded paper, and she chose to return it now. Fenn restored one unspent seed to the allotment, making eleven. “There are eleven now,” Sera said. The return did not restore either memory freely given to the two seeds opened yesterday. It added the separately held glass to the ten now in the case. Sera wrote the transfer beside the old loan and asked Fenn to add her mark. Orin watched the account distinguish a new receipt from a reversal of the past and asked whether every page in the memory book could be made so clear.

Fenn did not answer at once. Fenn put the memory book into Sera’s hands. The volume was heavier than Sera expected, swollen with leaves that had been pasted over older leaves. The blank page was warm even in the cold cistern air. Sera opened to it carefully, keeping her bound palm clear of the edge. Beneath the blank surface lay the shadow of an entry scraped thin enough to remove its words but not its heat. Mael called it an old binding fault. Orin asked him how he knew which page she had opened. He said everyone could feel the warmth. Neither Fenn nor Orin had mentioned it outside the library. Sera left the inconsistency beside his explanation without selecting a verdict. Sera suspected the blank page belonged to a memory Mael had taken. The suspicion gave her a reason to inspect the earlier index. It was not permission to write his name into every empty space.

The bell touched the cistern floor with a soft sound unlike any note Sera had heard from it above ground. They lowered the bronze bell into the cistern. Orin held the rope taut while she set the loose seed beside the rim. The ringing seed answered the bell inside the cistern. The answering tone made dust move across the dry stone. Mael took one step down. Orin asked him to wait until they had measured the space between seed and metal. The reeve stopped, furious at being delayed by a practical question he could not plausibly forbid. Sera knew a freely offered memory was required before the seed would open. Sound did not supply consent, however familiar a seed found the note. Sera repeated this before anybody could call the ringing a command to open it. Fenn nodded, then looked away from the warm page as though agreement had exposed a memory she would rather not volunteer.

“I never gave the orchard a memory,” Fenn said. Fenn spoke so abruptly that Sera first thought she was answering a question asked days earlier. The index contradicted her. A small signature beside an early offering matched the mark she had just made in the allotment book, and the note described a daughter learning to whistle through a reed. Sera asked whether she denied the signature. Fenn said the gift had been made before the orchard belonged to a reeve. That explained why she might wish to place it outside the present dispute; it did not make never accurate. She allowed Sera to copy the page and said she had hoped silence would keep the child's name safe. Orin set the rope down while she spoke, giving the account the same attention he had given a fragile bell.

The name appeared again where a patch of mineral crust had lifted from the wall. A child’s name appeared beneath the cistern’s mineral crust. Sera brushed around it without touching the strokes, afraid that enthusiasm would erase what drought had revealed. Fenn recognised it and sat on the lowest step. Mael said children scratched names everywhere. Fenn answered that this child had died before the cistern was completed. Her report established her recognition; the dated offering beside the same name provided a second connection. Sera did not write that every mark in the chamber belonged to a dead child. She copied this one, its position, and the page number. Mael offered to bring a council witness in the morning. Sera asked why they needed to wait until he could choose who accompanied them. The question hung in the cool chamber without the comfort of an immediate answer.

A crack sounded above them, followed by the scrape of wood along stone. Orin climbed first. Sera reached the orchard as the last branch struck the wall. The last living branch snapped; the old tree was dead. The small green line she had found yesterday had turned brown at its centre. Fenn examined the broken surface and shook her head before Mael could repeat his promise. Orin believed the old tree could still be revived, although every root had gone cold. He wanted to ring the bell and ask for a stronger gift. Sera said a stronger gift could bring rain to a sapling; it could not make the broken tree the same living tree it had been. She hated saying this while its leaves still looked almost ordinary. The world offered no change of colour dramatic enough to make the rule feel fair. Orin put his hand on the rough trunk and left it there until the others stopped speaking.

Mael removed the glove when they returned to the cistern. A pale scar crossed his palm in the old keeper's pattern, and he signed the blank line in the book's damaged index. Mael’s signed confession identified him as a former keeper of the memory orchard. He had taken custody of memories under promises he later called inconvenient, then scraped the names away so nobody could ask what had been kept. The seeds would not accept a forced gift, but people could still be deceived into giving freely on false terms. His first account called that misunderstanding. Fenn asked him to write the terms he had offered, not the name he preferred for breaking them. If the glove concealed a keeper’s scar, Mael might have opened the first seed. The scar made the possibility worth investigating; it did not date every seed he had ever touched. Sera copied his signed account and marked the unanswered questions below it.

Orin had gone to fetch the smaller tools they would need to lift the mineral crust without breaking its letters. Orin waited in the village square with his tools. Before leaving he asked Sera whether she still wanted him to keep helping after the mistake he had made about the old tree. She said being wrong about a wish was different from concealing a gift. Sera and Orin agreed to share responsibility for every voluntary gift. They could check the count, explain the cost, and let each giver decline without being blamed for the drought. Fenn believed the council would hear Sera before sunset. Sera hoped the council would listen, but the hope did not count as a hearing already held. She meant to ask every household for a voluntary memory the next morning. The household visits belonged to tomorrow. Tonight Fenn could decide whether she wanted the old name restored to the book, and Mael could answer questions in the presence of a witness he had not selected himself.

While Fenn rested, Sera sat on the step where a high-water line crossed her ankles. Sera recalled the first chapter’s visit to the seed library, before the cistern gates opened. That was the first visit in this sequence of events, before she had seen the cistern floor or understood why the warm page frightened Fenn. Recalling the room did not move her back into it. She was below the orchard now, holding the book and listening to the bell settle after a faint shift in the rope. She understood why an account might contain both a former location and a present one without asking a later reader to choose which was real. Both had been real at different times. Mael asked whether she would cross out his former title in the index. She said she would add what had changed and keep what explained the earlier pages. He looked more troubled by that answer than by an accusation.

Darkness reached the cistern slowly. Sera slept with the book wrapped beneath her head and the seed case still in Fenn's custody on the step above. She dreamed the cistern filled with voices instead of water. Every voice asked for rain and none would say which memory belonged to it. When she woke, the chamber was dry. The sound had come from Orin lowering a tool basket, not from water arriving while she slept. Fenn said she was going to the surface for air and would return with a lamp. Mael sat where the witnesses could see him. The old tree had not revived. Sera ran one finger over the unopened allotment page, counted the eleven intact circles, and left room for the first gift that someone would choose without a promise made on their behalf. Sera waited on the dry floor of the cistern for Fenn to return.

details.text:
They put the seed table in the square where people could approach it from any side. Sera refused the reeve's raised chair and used the bench normally reserved for repairing baskets. A person ought to be able to leave without appearing to walk away from a throne. Fenn brought the case after the households had heard the terms in private. Fenn returned the seed case to Sera. Sera checked all eleven seeds with her and closed the lid again before anyone made an offering. Orin hung a small unpolished bell on the table's end. It could call for attention, but Sera told the gathering that silence would count as silence, never as consent. Mael stood among the other villagers without his ceremonial coat. The silver glove lay on the council table beside the signed account of what he had taken.

The council read its decision in a voice made uncertain by the lack of a customary formula. The council recorded Mael’s resignation and named him former reeve. He would return the records he had concealed and answer for the households misled by their altered terms. Nobody announced that returning a book would repair every loss recorded inside it. Fenn asked for that sentence to be included, and the clerk repeated it slowly enough for the listeners at the back to hear. “I thought borrowing a memory was harmless,” Mael said. Mael offered the thought as an explanation, and Sera allowed it that place without allowing it to become an acquittal. He had used borrowing for a transaction whose ending only he could choose. The council's task was to change that power, not simply exchange his preferred word for a harsher one. The clerk left a place beneath the decision where any household could add its own account.

Orin offered first. He described making the old bell from household metal and hearing his daughter recognise the shape of her grandmother's pot in its rim. He asked Sera to wait while he considered whether he wished to give that particular memory. The waiting felt long enough for the whole square to become uncomfortable, which made it useful. At last he nodded and touched the seed. The ringing seed held Orin’s freely offered memory. The tone had answered him in the cistern because a true gift had been offered to that seed long before the reeve removed its label. Today he freely confirmed it after hearing the full cost. Rain opened above the table and moved towards the orchard in a narrow shining band. Nobody applauded until Orin chose to step away, and then Fenn asked them to leave the quiet intact for the next giver.

Mael brought the warm page to Fenn with both hands empty. It had held the remembered reed whistle after the name was scraped away, preserving the gift as an unclaimed object instead of letting the giver decide what followed. The warm page returned the memory Mael had taken. Fenn read the restored lines and spoke the name she had refused to speak in the cistern. The child’s name belonged to the memory’s rightful giver. Sera had expected a dramatic change in the air. Instead the page cooled, and Fenn remembered a small mistake in the tune that she had not known she had forgotten. Fenn had believed silence would protect the child’s name, but silence had protected Mael instead. The restored name did not bring the child back, and nobody suggested spending a seed as if rain could do that. Fenn asked for a chair away from the table. Sera gave her one and left the next question unasked until the old woman looked up again.

The scar beneath the glove had matched the keeper's mark in the oldest council drawing. The glove concealed the scar of the former keeper. Sera put that drawing beside the signed confession rather than offer the scar alone as proof of every accusation. A wound could identify a history without confessing what its owner had done in every year since. Mael said the first keeper had taught him that the orchard belonged to the village. Fenn answered that belonging to a village did not mean belonging to its reeve. They copied the distinction into the new rules. The village library took custody of the memory book. The custody record named the shelf, the hours of access, and the conditions under which a giver could ask for a page to be read in private. Sera liked its awkward specificity. A generous general promise had served them badly. This one would require a person to open a door at a stated time.

Two other villagers offered memories after the first rain ended. One declined halfway through the explanation, and the square allowed her to return to her basket without making her refusal part of the drought's blame. Sera checked with each of the two who continued, then used a separate seed for each gift. Sera released three seeds and closed the case on eight. “Eight seeds remain,” Sera said. She wrote the three spent seeds below the eleven received from Fenn and showed the count to Orin. The unused glass remained intact, neither a debt already paid nor a harvest they could assume would happen. The rain darkened the ground beside the old stump. A new sapling was alive beside the dead stump. Its leaves were smaller than Sera's thumb and too new to resemble the crown that had stood there yesterday. Sera knew the new sapling was not the old tree restored. She made herself say the distinction aloud, because grief made resemblance more persuasive than a written rule.

Orin took his tools back through the orchard gate. Orin returned to the orchard to hang a smaller bell. The smaller bell would sound near the sapling, far enough from the dead trunk that nobody could mistake which living thing it served. Orin believed the new sapling would need ordinary care as well as rain. Water would help, but so would a stake, a fence against hungry goats, and someone noticing when the shade became too deep. Sera found that list comforting. Ordinary care did not require a person to discover a more precious memory each time a leaf wilted. Sera trusted Orin to teach the next apprentice without concealing the cost. He agreed that no apprentice should have to guess which part of a gift had been concealed from its giver. The promise was his, and she would still write the procedure down. Trust could make a written account less suspicious without making it unnecessary. He took a blank page from the clerk before returning to the gate.

The old bronze bell remained in the village square. People walked around it on their way to the well, touching the rough place that had once been a cooking pot. Sera stood in the village square when the first new rain fell. The rain was slight enough that dust remained beneath the benches, and the old cistern would need more than a ceremony to fill. Beyond the roofs a cloud gathered over the western ridge. Sera could not know whether the distant cloud had been made by their seeds. A natural cloud and a seed-made shower could occupy the same sky without announcing their origins to an apprentice. She wrote where the rain had first touched the square, because she had seen that. She did not draw a border around the cloud and claim it as the village's work. Mael watched her leave the line unfinished. For once he did not offer to finish it with a confident explanation.

Fenn sat beside the table after most of the villagers had gone. She asked what Sera remembered of the travelling potter who had taught her before the orchard apprenticeship. Sera recalled an apprenticeship with a travelling potter, though she could not remember when it began. Sera could recall the shape of his cart wheel and the way he tested a bowl by tapping it with a fingernail. The year and the first lesson remained beyond reach. She did not know whether the missing date had ever belonged to a spent seed or simply to the ordinary disorder of childhood. Fenn said she did not have to choose a magical explanation for every gap. They talked about clay for a while. It felt almost disloyal to enjoy a subject that did not solve the orchard, and then Sera decided that a village worth saving would need room for conversations that solved nothing urgent at all.

The clerk brought the new allotment book for her signature. She intended to teach the next apprentice to keep a written account. She wanted the next child entrusted with the case to know that a quantity could increase by a corrected count, decrease through an opened seed, and remain unchanged by a wish. If every gift remained voluntary, the orchard might never demand another debt. It was a hope about the future, not a weather report or a guarantee that nobody would deceive a giver again. The clerk wrote the conditional form as she spoke it. Fenn looked over the page and asked for a larger space beside the word declined. People should be able to refuse in more than a narrow margin. Sera drew the column wider and copied the page again, though it meant admitting the first neat version had been insufficient. The abandoned sheet became a cover for the seedlings instead of a record anyone had to defend.

She slept briefly beneath the square's awning while Fenn watched the locked case. She dreamed of a kitchen in which nobody had forgotten the door. The shelves were filled with bowls that kept their shapes, and a voice from another room asked whether she was ready to eat. On waking she heard an ordinary cart turning near the well. The old tree remained dead, the new sapling remained small, and the eight unopened seeds waited for choices nobody had yet made. She retrieved the case from beside Fenn's chair without changing its count. The awning had begun to drip at one corner. Sera moved the book away from the water, set a basin beneath the drip, and listened to a few drops fall without asking whose memory had purchased them. Sera remained in the village square beside the seed table.
